analysis.one_liner: Taxes stock, bond, and derivative trades up to 0.5%, with the tax rebated to low-income households.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 24 House Democrats, never received a hearing or vote and died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a small tax on every purchase of stocks, bonds, partnership interests, and derivatives: 0.5% of the value of a stock trade, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives. High-frequency trading firms that buy and sell thousands of times a day would bear the largest share, while households earning under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples) would get the tax back as a credit. The bill does not earmark the money, but its stated purpose is to fund public programs like child care, infrastructure, health coverage, and clean energy, and its backers say such a tax could raise hundreds of billions of dollars a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income households, who would get the tax refunded through a credit, plus the programs the revenue could fund — child care, Social Security, infrastructure, Medicare and Medicaid expansion, housing assistance, and climate investment. The bill's findings argue the tax would also curb high-frequency trading, which it says accounts for up to 70% of market volume and adds volatility. Ordinary investors making occasional trades would pay at most a few dollars per trade and could get the amount back.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.5% tax on stock transfers, 0.1% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives, collected by exchanges and brokers rather than individual traders
Refunds the full tax paid as a credit to individuals with modified adjusted gross income up to $50,000 ($75,000 for joint filers), adjusted for inflation
Exempts initial stock and bond issuances, short-term debt maturing within 60 days, municipal bonds, and securities lending, so new capital raising is not taxed
The bill's findings cite economists' estimates that such a tax could generate hundreds of billions annually for public investment, and notes the U.S. levied a similar transfer tax from 1914 to 1966

analysis.who_pays: The financial industry: high-frequency trading firms, hedge funds, banks, and other large institutions that trade constantly, whose costs would rise the most per dollar of profit. Exchanges and brokers would be responsible for collecting the tax. Households above the income limits who trade securities would also pay without a rebate, and some of the tax would likely be passed through to investors in funds and retirement accounts in the form of slightly higher trading costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-frequency traders and large financial firms

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every covered purchase, including trades inside mutual funds and retirement portfolios, so some cost would reach ordinary savers through higher fund trading expenses

The bill's own findings put revenue estimates at 'hundreds of billions annually' per economists, but the bill attaches no official revenue score, and trading volume may fall as firms trade less to avoid the tax
The bill raises revenue but does not itself direct any of it to a specific program, so the promised spending on child care, infrastructure, and health would depend on later appropriations

The bill imposes penalties on taxpayers who fail to report covered transactions and gives the IRS Commissioner authority to rescind penalties without judicial review, which raises due-process concerns

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside is large: a recurring revenue stream of potentially hundreds of billions a year from the most active financial traders, with an explicit rebate protecting households under the income caps from bearing the cost. The main honest objections are that the burden would partly reach ordinary savers through fund and retirement-account trading costs, that actual revenue depends on how much trading volume shrinks in response, and that the bill guarantees no spending — only a funding source. A well-designed version could deliver real public revenue at modest cost to everyday investors; the design here attempts to address the pass-through with the credit but cannot fully eliminate it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or markup, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the bill on April 21, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation
24 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-frequency trading firms, banks, hedge funds, and other large financial institutions that would have paid the tax on every trade are better off, along with their investors, because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tax on Wall Street Speculation Act and recruited 10 original cosponsors

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Richard Neal, D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 25 supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the decisive obstacle was inaction by the Democratic-chaired Ways and Means Committee, which never took the bill up.

industries.industry: High-frequency trading and proprietary trading firms
industries.note: These firms execute trades constantly, so even a 0.5% tax per purchase would compound into their largest cost, and the bill's findings say the tax is partly aimed at curbing high-frequency trading. Their interest in blocking the tax runs directly against the revenue's intended public use.

industries.industry: Banks, hedge funds, and asset managers
industries.note: Every purchase of stocks, bonds, or derivatives they make would be taxed, and brokers would bear responsibility for collecting it. Some of the cost would pass through to fund and retirement-account investors.

They would be legally responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on transactions on their facilities, adding compliance work, while higher trading costs could slightly reduce their trading volume.
